{
  "question_intent": "Request for examples and explanation of loan pricing improvements, loan spreads, and competitive positioning, as well as RWA efficiencies and future plans in the Investment Bank.",
  "main_topics": ["US Consumer Bank performance", "loan pricing and spreads", "RWA efficiencies", "Investment Bank strategy"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": true,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "I just wanted to understand better that improvement in performance, you called out improving in loan pricing and also in fees. The revenue share agreements, some of them were renegotiated. Can you maybe give us examples of how much the loan yields or loan spreads might have gone up or how you compare to competition? Something that would give us a better sense of how sustainable that is? I don't know if higher pricing might affect volume? Any examples of those two things that can help us get our head around that? And the second question is on the Investment Bank, you touched on it already, the RWA efficiencies. There's more to go, but if we think about the next plan or going forward, is the philosophy still to keep RWAs flat in the business? And if that's the case, I don't know if you can help us quantify those efficiencies in particular in [Global Markets], because I realise M&A and ECM don't really carry that much capital. Just to get a feeling of how much more room there is.",
  "answer_quote": "So on USCB, I mean the improvement that you are seeing coming through does come in large part from pricing. So, to give you an idea, the year-on-year improvements in NIM, about half of that comes from the repricing that we did last year, and that repricing was completed by the end of 2024. But the way this works through into the NIM is that consumers have to repay and then draw down on the new terms and conditions for that to really feed through into the NIM. There has been wider repricing across the market. That came initially from the expectations of late fee reductions last year and has not yet reversed. The impact for us in terms of late fees was relatively small, as you can imagine, relative to some of our competitors. And therefore, we don't believe that it's creating any kind of NIM competitive pressure. For some of our competition late fees would be more significant and therefore that might be more of a question. But on another level, one of the things that we established as we prepared for our strategy pre-February 2024, was we were not optimised for pricing, even on a like-for-like basis, even pre the loss of late fees. So, much of this has been a bit of an industry catch up and therefore has not really had a significant impact, in terms of competitive positioning. So, we remain comfortable where we are positioned and we do see it as sustainable in terms of the pricing. I mean the other things that are directly impacting the NIM are the growth in retail deposits. Remember there's a 50 to 60 basis points differential there [versus wholesale lending] and also the general expansion towards retail balances. Now, clearly in the quarter, there's only been one month of General Motors. So revenue sharing arrangements, I'm not going to call any of them out. We never do as a partner matter and they do actually impact both the NIM line and the non-NII line. So that's why you're seeing some improvements there also, as well as there being just generally increased volumes. So, underlying your question, is this sustainable? The answer is yes, we do believe it is, which is why we said we expected NIM to be broadly stable from here. Just remember it is quite a seasonal business, so you get some lumps and bumps particularly in Non-NII. So we're happy with that general direction. If I go onto the Investment Bank, what you've seen for the last six quarters is that the revenue over RWAs continues to improve. So, if you look year-over-year across those six quarters, you can see a step change each time and clearly what we were looking for at the beginning of the plan was the area where revenue over RWAs had declined markedly over time, [which] was really in the Banking business. And that's where we see a lot of the improvements starting to come through in very, very good capital discipline in driving that Treasury Coverage model. So, you can see that in the International Corporate Bank balances that are growing, and the income there, but also really being focused in M&A and ECM and as I called out before, we do feel there's more to go in those businesses. So in terms of the Banking business, you would expect there to be further road to travel in terms of this revenue over RWAs, because of the International Corporate Bank business continuing to perform. Just because we still have ambitions within ECM and M&A, that they remain a focus for us, but also just this kind of real discipline about the maturation of capital and really whether we continue to extend it to that client or not, or choose to put it elsewhere. So much more to go, I think tangibly within Banking. But in the Markets business, clearly that was coming from a slightly different place. It wasn't a situation where we deployed more capital into that business and that it had largely maintained its revenue over RWAs. What you're seeing now is it continuing to improve because it is taking share, and in many instances we'd already given capital to those focus businesses and they're sort of growing into the capital and maturing into that capital. And then the other thing is obviously Financing, a very capital light business, continues to grow, particularly on the Prime side where the balances were 30% up year on year. So, I can't give you a specific target and indeed that's not how we're thinking about this business in particular, because we do think of it in terms of RoTE. So, it's a number of things to get there, but think of us as still feeling like there's room to go in terms of that revenue over RWAs.",
